Moving to NYC

What is the cost of moving to NYC?

Enter your current ZIP code in the free calculator below to price the movers' share of the cost of moving to NYC for your home.

20+ years in the moving business

  • Home or apartment

Where are you moving?

Two ZIP codes give us the distance and the type of move.

Estimator's noteShort moves are usually billed by the hour for the crew and truck. Long moves are priced by the weight of your things and the distance. Your ZIP codes decide which applies.

Your price shows before we ask for any contact details.

Moving the contents of a 1-bedroom apartment to New York City from about 1,000 road miles away costs $1,400–$3,300 with a long-distance mover, off peak, with no stairs or extras. From New Jersey or Long Island, about 10 road miles, the same apartment costs $380–$960. That is the movers' share of the cost of moving to NYC. A lease adds its own upfront bill: the first month's rent and a security deposit.

The two bills behind the cost of moving to NYC

Think of the cost of moving to NYC as two bills. The first gets your belongings to the city: a moving company, a rental truck or a portable container. The second gets you the keys: a first month's rent, a security deposit and the smaller fees that come with a lease. In a city where most households rent, that second bill is often the larger one, so budget for both before you pick a moving date.

The calculator above prices the first bill from your own ZIP code and home size. The sections below show how a mover prices a move into the city from far away and from close by, what a landlord can and can't charge you, and what to plan for in your first month.

Shipping your belongings to the city from another state

From hundreds of miles away, a mover prices your shipment by its weight and the road miles, not by the hour. Jacksonville and St. Louis are each a little under 1,000 road miles from Manhattan, close to the distance the long-distance figures here assume. Off peak, with no stairs or extras, the cost of moving to NYC from that far runs:

  • a studio apartment: $1,150–$2,350;
  • a 1-bedroom apartment: $1,400–$3,300;
  • a 2-bedroom apartment: $2,600–$5,700.

The city end can push those figures up. A walk-up adds flights of stairs, a doorman building may allow move-ins only at set hours, and a truck that can't stand at the door means a long carry down the block. Where a full-size truck can't reach the street, the mover may move your things to a smaller shuttle truck, which is charged on top. Tell every mover about each of these conditions, so the written estimate prices them into the cost of moving to NYC.

Federal rules require an interstate mover to give you a written estimate. A binding estimate fixes the price unless you add items or services. Under a non-binding estimate, the mover can't require you to pay more than 110 percent of it at delivery. FMCSA explains both kinds of estimate. Expect a delivery window of several days, too, and plan where you'll sleep if your lease starts before your things arrive.

Moving in from New Jersey, Long Island or Westchester

Many newcomers arrive from close by, and a short move is priced by the crew's time rather than by weight. A 1-bedroom apartment moved 10 road miles costs $380–$960, and a 2-bedroom $720–$1,800, off peak, with no stairs or extras. In the rate table behind the calculator, the same 1-bedroom at 30 road miles costs roughly 15 to 20 percent more. Ask how the mover bills bridge and tunnel tolls, since those add to the cost of moving to NYC from the suburbs.

The state line matters more than the miles. A move from Jersey City or Hoboken to Manhattan is short, but it crosses into New York, so it is an interstate move and the mover needs a USDOT number. FMCSA's Protect Your Move pages show how to look one up. A move from Long Island, Westchester or upstate stays inside New York, so the mover needs a license from the state instead. The crew table below shows how the hours and the total change with the size of the crew.

What a lease adds to the cost of moving to NYC

For many renters, the lease is the larger part of the cost of moving to NYC. Most landlords ask for these before you sign or on signing day:

  • The first month's rent, often by certified check or bank transfer.
  • A security deposit. New York law caps it at one month's rent, and the landlord must return it, less lawful deductions, after you move out.
  • A broker fee, only if you hired the broker. Since June 11, 2025, New York City's FARE Act has barred a broker who represents the landlord from charging you. If you hire your own broker to search for you, you pay that broker.
  • A background and credit check. State law bans application fees and caps what a landlord may charge for this check.
  • Renters insurance, which many buildings require before you move in.

Landlords also check your income. Many look for yearly income of about 40 times the monthly rent, or a guarantor who earns about 80 times. If you fall short, a guarantor company can back the lease for a fee. Add each of these to the movers' range, and the cost of moving to NYC becomes a figure you can save toward.

Ship it, sell it or buy it in the city

City apartments tend to have fewer bedrooms than homes elsewhere, and the homes panel below compares New York City's mix with the whole US. A smaller new place changes the math. Every piece you ship adds weight and miles, and a sofa that won't fit up a narrow stair costs you twice. Measure your new doorways, halls and stairwells before you decide what goes.

On a long haul, selling a bulky piece and buying again in the city can beat shipping it. Keep what is costly to replace or hard to find, and let go of what is cheap to buy and heavy to carry. Each piece you leave behind trims the cost of moving to NYC twice: once on the truck, and again on the carry up to your floor.

Your first month in the city

The cost of moving to NYC doesn't end when the truck pulls away. Plan for these too:

  • Tips for the crew: moving guides suggest $20.00–$65.00 per mover per working day for a local crew and $40.00–$100.00 for a long-distance one, as typical published figures.
  • Getting around: most residents ride the subway and buses, and keeping a car means paying for parking.
  • Utilities and internet: set them up in your name before move-in day, and ask whether the provider wants a deposit.
  • Your license and car: the New York DMV gives new residents 30 days to exchange an out-of-state license and 30 days to register a vehicle they bring.
  • Furniture and basics: a mattress, kitchen things and whatever you sold before you left.

Pinning down your own cost of moving to NYC

Four steps turn the cost of moving to NYC from a guess into a figure you can plan around:

  1. Price the movers' share in the calculator above. It's free, takes about a minute and needs no email to see your price.
  2. Ask two or three movers for written estimates after a video or in-home survey, and tell each about the stairs, elevators and truck parking at both ends.
  3. Check a USDOT number for a move from another state, or a New York license for a move from within the state.
  4. Add the lease's upfront costs and a cushion for your first month.

Set that total beside your savings before you sign a lease. The movers' range and the lease's upfront costs together are the cost of moving to NYC for your household, and knowing both lets you choose a date, an apartment and a mover you can afford.

Key takeaways

The main numbers on this page, in a few lines.

  • New York City's five counties had 266 moving companies with paid employees in 2023: 3.1 per 100,000 residents, against 2.8 across the US.
  • The New York State Department of Transportation licenses motor carriers for hire operating within the state, and oversees household goods movers' rates and services.
  • Keep commercial trucks off home streets from 9 PM to 5 AM (NYC311).
  • In New York City, 1 in 10 people moved in the last year, against 1 in 8 across the US.
  • The most common home in New York City has 2 bedrooms: 32% of homes, against 25% across the US.
  • With 3 movers, a 2-bedroom home move takes about 4–6.5 hours on site: $720–$1,800 off peak at 10 road miles.
  • In New York City, May, September and October are the mildest, driest months to move, by NOAA's 30-year averages.
  • More households moved to New York City's five counties from Nassau County, NY than from any other county in 2022-2023: 8,738.
  • The cost of moving to NYC has two parts: getting your things to the city, and the upfront costs of a lease.
  • A New York landlord can ask for no more than one month's rent as a security deposit.
  • Since June 11, 2025, a renter in New York City pays a broker fee only to a broker the renter hired.
  • A move from New Jersey crosses a state line, so the mover needs a USDOT number even for a few miles.

New York's license for moves within the state

Coming from Long Island, Westchester or upstate keeps the move inside New York, so this license applies to the cost of moving to NYC from there. It shows which state agency licenses movers, and what it oversees.

The New York State Department of Transportation licenses motor carriers for hire operating within the state, and oversees household goods movers' rates and services.

Source: New York State Department of Transportation, "Registration & Licensing" (read 2026-10-28)

For interstate moves, from one state to another, the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration requires a U.S. DOT number; for moves within a state, requirements vary.

Street rules your moving truck meets on arrival

Where a truck may stand and which roads it may use can add billed hours, and hours add to the cost of moving to NYC. These city rules each name their source and the day they were last checked.

Keep commercial trucks off home streets from 9 PM to 5 AM

Commercial vehicles cannot park on residential streets overnight, between 9 PM and 5 AM. Vehicles in violation may be issued a parking violation.

Source: NYC311, checked 28 October 2026

Keep the truck off the parkways

Trucks and commercial vehicles cannot travel on most parkways in New York City. NYC DOT publishes a list of the parkways where they are prohibited, and a truck route map.

Source: NYC DOT, checked 28 October 2026

Questions

What is the cost of moving to NYC? FAQ

Can't find your answer? Email hello@liftmyboxes.com.

How much money should you save before moving to NYC?

Start with the movers' range for your home and route, then add the first month's rent, a security deposit of up to one month's rent, and a broker fee only if you hire your own broker. Movers alone charge $380–$960 for a 1-bedroom moved 10 road miles, off peak, with no stairs or extras. Keep a cushion of a few months' living costs on top, because most of the cost of moving to NYC is paid before your first paycheck.

Is there a calculator for the cost of moving to NYC?

Yes. The calculator at the top of this page prices the movers' share of the cost of moving to NYC from your ZIP code, for your home size and date. It's free and needs no email. Add the lease's upfront costs to its range for the full figure.

Do you still pay a broker fee to rent in New York City?

Only if you hire the broker yourself. Since June 11, 2025, the FARE Act has barred brokers who represent the landlord from charging the tenant. Listings must also disclose any fees a tenant will pay.

What salary do you need to rent an apartment in NYC?

Many New York landlords look for yearly income of about 40 times the monthly rent, or a guarantor who earns about 80 times. If you don't meet that, a guarantor company can back the lease for a fee. Count that fee in the cost of moving to NYC if you are starting a new job in the city.

How long does a long-distance delivery to NYC take?

Long-distance movers usually give a delivery window of several days rather than one fixed date, and a longer haul gets a wider window. Get the window in writing with the estimate. If your lease starts first, plan a few nights on an air mattress or in a short-term rental.
